If this isn't enough to cause Direct Intervention to be placed AT THE VERY
TOP of the watch list for 2009 -- and hopefully banned in 2010 -- then
nothing ever will.

This guy gets 3GW/9VP with a well-made/metagamed deck, and loses... to a
stupid Direct Intervention. Wow, nice reward.

What Direct Intervention does is bad and wrong, as it stops people from
being able to play the game. (Yes, Sudden/Wash has a similar ability, but
you know damn well that the game is made to be played with library cards
being used by your minions, so please don't try to throw up straw men to
avoid the DI discussion.)

Thoughts Betrayed was changed because it used to say "You are unable to
play the game."

Protect Thine Own was banned because it says "You are unable to play the
game, in the most un-fun way the designers of this card game could think
of."

Direct Intervention is a silver bullet, and we all know it. Why is it
still part of this game??

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
"Obtenebration" <obtene...@obtenebration.org> wrote in message
news:6626250e-4e5b-4a65...@z11g2000prl.googlegroups.com...

> But yes I agree totally with the rationale to ban Direct Intervention.
> Any card that can be included in any deck since it requires a cost of
> simply a pool and a MPA,

1) A pool and an MPA is not an insignificant cost, especially when weighed
against the costless minion card that has to be tossed in the discard pile
and can even be replayed if the methuselah involved has another in hand.
It only looks powerful because people only discuss spectacular plays.

2) No one ever mentions the unseen cost - the hand space it takes up from
draw to play. If no worthwhile card pops up that warrants it, you can
effectively play with a 6-card hand for several turns waiting.

3) It has the usual cancel-card disadvantage in a multiplayer game. Guy
playing it pays an MPA and pool; guy it's played on loses a chance to play
an (ideally) key minion card. Three other methuselahs are the real
winners.

4) The comparison of PTO to Direct Intervention as unfun buzz-kill cards is
such utter bullshit as to not warrant response. Give me a break people
can't have fun with DI in the game! This card's been around since The
Sabbat and I have never figured out why some people get so bugged by it.
I swear, it's just weird!

Fred

Locally, I agree with you--no one around here plays DI all that much.
Once and a while, one will show up, and the end result is rarely
anything other than "I DI your Govern!" "Ok, I play another one..."

But on a competitive level, where folks regularly play 3 or 4 DIs per
deck, all the time, it is a complete nightmare. I have had many games
arbitrarily demolished by someone cross table DIing whatever I was about
to oust my prey with just 'cause they had one in hand and couldn't bear
to see me oust a prey (as it would "unbalance the table" or some crap
like that). In ways that most other cards simply could not effect.

That, and the incredibly endless "DI Phase" ("Huh. That's not good.
Should I DI that? Let me discuss it with everyone else at the table for
5 minutes...") of every action in competition is just completely
unnecessary. I hate DI. I have always hated DI. I would love to see it
vaporize instantly.

Messages.Author: Darby Keeney
Messages.Body:
On Sep 13, 1:08 am, "Frederick Scott" <nos...@no.spam.dot.com> wrote:

> 1) A pool and an MPA is not an insignificant cost, especially when weighed
> against the costless minion card that has to be tossed in the discard pile
> and can even be replayed if the methuselah involved has another in hand.
> It only looks powerful because people only discuss spectacular plays.

At it's simplest level, for my 1 pool and 1 MPA:

I DI a Conditioning.....I lose 2 less pool than I would have.
I DI a Wake/bounce....I lose 0-7 less pool, my predator loses 0-7
more.
I DI a KRC/ConAgg/RecklessAgit. I lose 2-5 less pool and stuff my
predator's hand with unplayable action modifiers.
I DI a voter cap, leaving a minion nearly to completely empty and
costing someone (my prey?) 2 pool.
I DI a stealth, allowing a block, saving 1-8 pool and allowing me to
possibly kick the crap out of your minion.
I DI your crux minion card in action "x", preventing an oust which
gains you 6 pool, and allows me to kill you (and then your former
prey)
I DI your agg damage weapon, neutering your defenses, hopefully long
enough for me to kill you.
I DI your grapple, allowing my minion to escape combat and act in my
turn.

AND THE ADDITIONAL OPTION OF...any of the above, applied for some
other methesulah of my choosing, with no additional/incremental cost.

All of these things look like reasonable bargains to me.

Of course, it doesn't mean things always work as I have outlined them
above.....just that this card has the POTENTIAL to do all of them.
Seems like a lot of function, rolled into 1 card. Fred said people
discuss the spectacular DI plays.....which happens with relatively
high frequency because the card is disproportionately powerful and
flexible.

Kevin called it a "silver bullet." - which might be more a propos for
a Werewolf game, but I'll accept the terminology :)

It is cancellation, intercept, denial of other's deck function and
facilitation of my deck function, all available in the same card.
Isn't a card being highly flexible and measure of it's power (Govern =
speed + pool + offense = good card). IMO, just as in Kevin's, DI just
does too much all in one card slot and in a way that CAN deny a player
the ability to play the game (which I believe is generally
unhealthy).

> 2) No one ever mentions the unseen cost - the hand space it takes up from
> draw to play.  If no worthwhile card pops up that warrants it, you can
> effectively play with a 6-card hand for several turns waiting.

The same "unseen cost" as any card you hold but cannot immediately
use. This "cost" has little to do with the relative power of the
card, which is the point of contention. But, as a comparison, then
let us also apply the same hidden cost to stealth if there are no
blocks, intercept if there's no stealth directed at you, delaying
tactics if there are no votes, S:CE if there are no combats and combat
cards if there are no combats.

If we were talking about a long chain of sequentially played cards, I
might be willing to concede some merit in tendency to self-handcuff
(e.g., Voter Cap is hard to play - you need a vote, maybe stealth,
maybe vote push and then the cap - likely running with quite a bit of
additional setup to make it happen - so I believe it should be
impactful when played).

But DI is an isolated card that you can pop out of your hand pretty
much at need - the price of such ease of play should be lower impact,
higher cost, and/or limited (once per game) usefulness. In fact, if
DI only cancelled ACTION cards, we wouldn't see nearly as much use,
nor as much discussion, as we do in the existing function.

I might also mention, if these travel in 2-4 instance-per-deck
numbers, you could simply toss the first 1-2 you find, until the game
starts to teeter and their use becomes more impactful - then the
hidden cost is "one DPA"

> 3) It has the usual cancel-card disadvantage in a multiplayer game.  Guy
> playing it pays an MPA and pool; guy it's played on loses a chance to play
> an (ideally) key minion card.  Three other methuselahs are the real
> winners.

No, I don't agree with that. If my DI stops someone from doing
something crucial at an important time and it significantly benefits
my table position (sometimes to the point of I get 1-2 more VPs, or
even simply stay alive for additional turns), I am the winner. At
that point, the other three methuselahs simply wish that their MPAs
were half as productive as mine was.

> 4) The comparison of PTO to Direct Intervention as unfun buzz-kill cards is
> such utter bullshit as to not warrant response.  Give me a break people
> can't have fun with DI in the game!  This card's been around since The
> Sabbat and I have never figured out why some people get so bugged by it.
> I swear, it's just weird!

The fact that the card has been around for a while is not relevant.
PTO, seat switching and Succubus Club had been in the game a long time
too. Maybe you were bugged by these, maybe not....but that didn't
change the fact that they were considered bad for the game by the
current rules team/designers.

Just as clarification, Kevin did not say DI makes the game un-fun (he
applied that to PTO, which is gone). He said DI was "bad, and
wrong." I agree with him.....when it comes to action/play denial,
Masters should stop Masters (Sudden/Wash), minions should stop minions
(block).

> Fred

Darby

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
"Darby Keeney" <darby....@gmail.com> wrote in message
news:6d91d495-99fa-4eda...@r66g2000hsg.googlegroups.com...


And yet I don't observe that you play with that many D.I.s, Darby? Why
is that?

It may help to consider that it's the MPA that I think a lot of people
undervalue, not really the one pool whose value is well understood.
The 'wait factor' and the point that these scenarios you throw up
in reality turn out to be far less common than one would think from
such an argument as you just made above. CCG arguments often go back
and forth between people throwing conjecture at each other - which is
far easier to construct than it is to prove (or to disprove, to be
fair).

> Of course, it doesn't mean things always work as I have outlined them
> above.....just that this card has the POTENTIAL to do all of them.
> Seems like a lot of function, rolled into 1 card. Fred said people
> discuss the spectacular DI plays.....which happens with relatively
> high frequency because the card is disproportionately powerful and
> flexible.

See, that's where I disagree with you - and frequently others who hate
D.I. And it's also the thing that makes me insanely curious why there's
such disagreement about it. Those who hate D.I. seem to see games as
this series of dramatic plays with lots and lots of momentous turning
points, any of which would be reversed with D.I.s thus proving what a
terribly overpowered card it is. I just don't see this in games. I
see lots of play that goes back and forth and occasionally some plays
that are very important but I just don't see that many of them which
I'd find worthwhile to hold a D.I. and pay the pool and the MPA for. I
actually see very few. I value the master cards I know will help me
far more consistently more highly than I value D.I.s in most cases, so
I find it hard to appreciate your point of view.

> > 4) The comparison of PTO to Direct Intervention as unfun buzz-kill cards is
> > such utter bullshit as to not warrant response. Give me a break people
> > can't have fun with DI in the game! This card's been around since The
> > Sabbat and I have never figured out why some people get so bugged by it.
> > I swear, it's just weird!
>
> The fact that the card has been around for a while is not relevant.

It's relevent in the sense of showing how long this argument has gone on -
since D.I. was originally printed - and how long I've felt that way about
people who complain about D.I.

> PTO, seat switching and Succubus Club had been in the game a long time
> too. Maybe you were bugged by these, maybe not....but that didn't
> change the fact that they were considered bad for the game by the
> current rules team/designers.

The argument that PTO was a buzz-kill and thus not a good card to have in
the game because it lessens the fun of the game is one I've always been
sympathetic to, if not in outright agreement with. I never thought PTO
was unbalanced but I agree that power balance is not the only reason that
a card should be considered for banishment.

Succubus Club required tech development before its problems were uncovered.
No one - to my knowledge - is suggesting anyone has suddenly developed new
tech for D.I. requiring reconsideration of its status. These are just the
same ol', same ol' arguments getting dragged out again.

> Just as clarification, Kevin did not say DI makes the game un-fun (he
> applied that to PTO, which is gone).

He actually did. To deny this would be to suggest that he made his
statements about PTO and Thoughts Betrayed as some sort of meaningless
rhetorical fog. That is, there had to be SOME point about comparing D.I.
to PTO and Thoughts Betrayed with the inference that we should make an
association and deem D.I. bad. You can't have it both ways. So don't ask.

Fred

Ahh, THIS is where the thread went. I dont get the whole thing about
changing the title. :)

First let me say that I agree with banning DI. Mostly because I am
usually at the receiving end of them in the whole "whoops, that ruined
your game" aspect. Soul gem decks getting set back a couple of turns
while looking for another Gem, freak drive decks stopped cold (for one
turn at least), etc. etc.

Then let me add that I have to agree with Fred (I think?) in that DI
will often play a very decisive factor in a game, but I cant remember
a lot of games where it has been the single determining factor to
losing/winning a game (in the way that PTO, Dramatic Upheaval,
succubus club did).
Same for this final. The fact that he had 2 garous DI'ed on the same

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
In article <cn3zk.4645$Dj1....@newsfe01.iad>,

"Frederick Scott" <nos...@no.spam.dot.com> wrote:
> See, that's where I disagree with you - and frequently others who hate
> D.I. And it's also the thing that makes me insanely curious why there's
> such disagreement about it. Those who hate D.I. seem to see games as
> this series of dramatic plays with lots and lots of momentous turning
> points, any of which would be reversed with D.I.s thus proving what a
> terribly overpowered card it is. I just don't see this in games. I
> see lots of play that goes back and forth and occasionally some plays
> that are very important but I just don't see that many of them which
> I'd find worthwhile to hold a D.I. and pay the pool and the MPA for. I
> actually see very few. I value the master cards I know will help me
> far more consistently more highly than I value D.I.s in most cases, so
> I find it hard to appreciate your point of view.

Well, there is always a lot of conjecture and stories to make points,
but when it comes down to simple "here is what the card does", here is
what I primarily object to about the card:

A) It allows for completely unrestricted meddling, ignoring the
predator/prey relationship. The guy cross table can DI my action
modifier to foil my action. Which when combined with the incredible
versatility of the card makes it way too powerful. If it were only
useable on your predator or prey? It would be much less egregious.

B) It has no limitations at all, when similar cards have significant
limitations. DI was designed by the same crack wacky design team that
made Protect Thine Own and Return to Innocence (well, presumably). In
another example of "Here is clearly what the current design team thinks
is balanced, and here is how this other old card is way over that
threshold" (see: PTO vs Auto da Fe), we have Direct Intervention, which
costs 1 pool and 1 MPA as an OOT Master, and cancels any minion card.
Then we have Vox Domini, which costs 1 pool and 1 MPA as an OOT Master,
and makes a poltical action fail. And is only playable once per game by
each player. So for the exact same cost (1 pool, 1 MPA, OOT), Vox Domini
has a similar effect but is *vastly* more restricted *and* only playable
once per game. Yes, there is a difference between "cancel a card" and
"make a vote fail" which is not insignificant (vote fails means action
is wasted, etc.). So it is arguably reasonable that the limited effect
(cancel only vote, not any card) is more powerful (vote fails, not card
cancelled). But then it *also* is saddled with only being playable once
per game. Which, for a card that is already very limited, is just a kick
in the teeth. The end result is, given the similarities between the
cards, why would anyone *ever* play Vox Domini instead of Direct
Intervention (this is not an invitation to dig up every possible corner
case where you would want a Vox Domini, but every single time I have
considered a Vox Domini in a deck? I put in DI instead)? The DI costs
exactly the same, has a similar (and often identical--if you DI the
vital vote push action card? The end result is identical to Vox Domini)
yet much more flexible effect. And can be used multiple times per game.
Vox Domini seems like it should be a strong card (it has a very strong
effect). But DI makes it virtually pointless. And Vox Domini is
apparently what the current (or currenter) design team feels is a
balanced effect for a 1 pool OOT Master that cancels something.
Indicating the Direct Intervention is over the curve of what the current
design team thinks is acceptable.

If Direct Intervention was, say, 1 pool OOT Master, cancel a minion card
played by your predator or prey, only playable once per game per
methuselah, it would still be a pain in the ass, but would at least be
*much* less "arbitrary king makery" and would fit into the current power
level scheme reasonably.



That's right it was the combination of both - not just the D.I.s. This
does not make it an overpowered card; just the right draw at the right
moment.

> preliminary rounds indicates that Second Trads were not a particular

Prior performance has nothing to do with the issue. As I pointed out
to David, other kinds of intercept decks wouldn't have required the
presence of a D.I. - they would have just shut that deck down pretty
much all the time they sat next to it. (For that matter, the Mike
Curtois weenie auspex thing deliberately contains a lot a Eagle's
Sights just to be able to control things like Garous he would likely
conclude need to never hit the table.) The point that it just happened
to be a deck which required help from an early D.I. to win the war makes
for a poor example of D.I.'s power. Other fortuitous early cards, like an
Info Highway or a Zillah's Valley might have changed the same equation.
Or even a Far Mastery or other ally killer or stealer (assuming he'd had
a minion to play one or a third party had gotten involved) could likewise
have changed that equation.

Assuming it's fair to characterize the metagame matchup as being about
one deck getting a Garou on the table which would often happen before
its neighbor got its intercept functioning and normally being able to
do so, then it's just a question of a fortunate toolbox card (or two
cards, in this case) popping up at the right time. That happens all the
time in this game. D.I.s are admittedly an extremely flexible toolbox
card in that sense, but as long as they're balanced overall it's a moot
point.

One of the problems I find with the argument against D.I. is that those
who complain about it never quite lodge a coherent complaint. They're
mad because it can be a critical factor in a lot of different varied
situations but don't want to see that this by itself doesn't make D.I.
an overpowered card. If it were, packing lots of them would always be
an easier path to victory. Yet year after year, many areas and many
players don't have a problem with it. That's why I think the problem
isn't really power. The problem is that some people just get very
irritated by the use of cancel cards to make a critical play. (Or a
critical counter-play to a critical play - which is the same thing.)

Fred

>Players everywhere want to win, don't you think? So if really good

>is truly broken, it should begin to take on a "universal" nature and you
>should eventually start to see it everywhere. If you don't, that's an
>indication you're looking at differences in popular styles of play from
>one area to another.

Everywhere, no.

Each metagame is different. Direct Intervention hits some deck styles
hard, but others less so. For example, if a successful player plays a
master-heavy deck, other players playing Direct Intervention won't
affect it much. e.g. if the key tech in a given deck is Toreador Grand
Ball, Direct Intervention won't help. There are a variety of decks
where non-minion cards play a very strong enabling role, with minion
cards being the icing on the cake.

Additionally, even very good players will disagree about the merits of
particular cards.

If you're looking for a particular strategy to turn up everywhere before
looking at it as a potential problem, you'll never get it. Look through
the cards that have been errata-ed or banned over the years because they
were causing significant issues, and there are pretty much none of them
that have had problems appearing everywhere. Where problems have
occurred, however, they've been looked at and addressed if LSJ and the
Design Team (or whoever else) thinks it appropriate.

This isn't an argument in favour of altering DI, nor an argument against
it. But looking for universal appearance of a problem before you can
address it means that the game would have taken a very different path -
look at the 7/7 rulings, and see how many people shouted "These cards
aren't a problem." Rightly or wrongly, the cards weren't appearing
everywhere and being a problem everywhere.

--
James Coupe

>
>DI my Daring the Dawn? OK. Here's a Dawn Operation.
>
>Or I guess you could be using "diversity" to mean "dependence on many
>things at once" instead of the normal meaning. If so, then, yeah,
>contrived long strict-ordering chains are more affected by DI than
>simple short order-insensitve chains, sure.

Although your point is well-made, it's not *just* about long-chain
combos / setup needing the right order.

In a toolboxy deck, you might (for example) hold a bleed modifier in
hand for a couple of turns, to play it at the right point. That point
comes, and you slap it down. It gets DI-ed.

As in your example, a diverse, relatively focused deck stands a fair
chance of having another bleed modifier to hand soon (maybe even
already), and quite possibly a different one - so your Foreshadowing
Destruction gets DI-ed but, no problem, here's a Threats.

In the toolboxy deck, I probably don't have that option coming along
reliably, and so it's harder to plan your turn knowing that your key
card might get DI-ed.

I'm not sure I'd want to classify all toolbox decks as being contrived
long strict-ordering chains. (Nor would I really want to classify
toolbox decks as being bad, or a poor choice to play.) I don't know if
there's a good way of enlarging the description to include toolboxes
appropriately in the simple short-chain vs contrived long-chain
situation.

all up and down the East Coast of the US, and yet I still supported
the ban, based on what was going on in Europe at the time... *Shrug*

shift the game into something "other than VTES". I won't call it
"broken", because I don't think that the power of the thing isn't the
real root problem... Like Succubus Club (but not as bad), multiple
DI's amplify the ability of two players to shut down a third's game
entirely, if that player's strategy relies at all upon minion cards
(most do). That's why I don't advocate a ban. Text like "a player
may be targeted once during that player's turn" would fix things just
fine IMO.

> looking at it as a potential problem, you'll never get it. Look through
> the cards that have been errata-ed or banned over the years because they
> were causing significant issues, and there are pretty much none of them
> that have had problems appearing everywhere.

The problem is, we've been so far past banning cards or changing cards
purely for power reasons that examples from the last 6 or 8 years don't
really qualify. Maybe Succubus Club may be the one example of what you
mean but it's hard for me to tell since that seemed to be a European
thing. (You are clearly right that this wasn't universal; I'm just
hedging about whether it could be described as an overpowered card.)
All or almost all cards banned since 2000 have had some elements of other
kinds of problems they caused the game and were not exactly banned
because they were too powerful in the sense of making it to easy to use
these cards to win games (and PTO certainly wasn't at all).

> Where problems have
> occurred, however, they've been looked at and addressed if LSJ and the
> Design Team (or whoever else) thinks it appropriate.

Sure.

> This isn't an argument in favour of altering DI, nor an argument against
> it. But looking for universal appearance of a problem before you can
> address it means that the game would have taken a very different path -
> look at the 7/7 rulings, and see how many people shouted "These cards
> aren't a problem." Rightly or wrongly, the cards weren't appearing
> everywhere and being a problem everywhere.

I definitely take your meaning about the 7/7 Rulings and other things
like it (the Anarch Revolt reprint changes is another good example).
But understand that I'm responding to charges that D.I. is broken because
you can't go to certain places in the world without encountering people
having 4+ of them in every deck combined with the statement that D.I. is
clearly broken because of what you can use it to accomplish when you
conjecture the perfect situation and get the perfect result (e.g. Darby's
list). It's been a long time since we've had something as broken as
Tomb of Ramses III or Return to Innocence but I think these would demonstrate
universal power problems in the game.

My concern about accepting the idea that certain "Direct Intervention trouble
spots" indicate the card is a problem is that I suspect there are probably
play styles in the game which might tend to be very successful in heavy D.I.
environments if the card is so ubiquitous as people claim. On the other hand,
perhaps there is some dynamic at work in those places which I'm unqualified to
judge without going there. I don't know.

What I *do* know is that at least three people who frequently play in
tournaments where I play (Los Angeles) have complained about D.I. I've seen
enough play in Los Angeles to feel pretty confident in saying that Direct
Intervention has never been demonstrated to be an overpowered crutch card there.
This makes me suspect that said players have a problem with the character of the
card and not its power, as they claim. This, in turn, makes me a bit skeptical
about whether D.I.'s popularity elsewhere is a matter of utility or simply
play style. The obvious implication is that it's play style - and consequently
is creating a lot of frustration in terms of game speed but isn't really
overpowered there either. If so, there may be *some* kind of a problem - but
not a power problem.

Fred

> A) a master card and
> B) a minion card

I think I'd go with A.
For a DI to have a good effect you need to know some stuff about the
deck/player you use it against imo. In casual games where I know
exactly what card to cancel and when, the effect is huge. I know it
would be pointless to cancel a Govern against my friend since it's
more than likely he's got 2+ more on his hand, so instead I cancel the
Conditioning safely knowing that there's no more than 2 Foreshadowing
Destruction in the deck...
Against a deck I've never seen before it's much harder to do the right
thing if you're thinking about whether to cancel the Govern or not.
There might not even be any more modifiers in the deck at all.

A master card is usually much easier to tell. A Minion Tap for 8 is
quite clear. That's 8 pool to your prey unless you cancel it. Blood
Dolls/Vessels as well. And as it has been pointed out earlier in the
thread, master cards are usually the biggest source of pool gain in a
deck.
So for a moderatly skilled player I'd say that picking the right
master card to cancel is much easier than cancelling the right minion
card.

Proper timing for DI on any card play: as the card is played.

There is the reality that the decks with the most room for
counterspells are the decks with the most efficient game plan. Is the
awesomeness rating of a tight stealth bleed deck with a suite of
counterspells due to the stealth bleed or the counterspells or the
combination?

The only time I tested the idea of doing something like 75 card deck (!
Malk SB back in the day when Malks didn't have Dementation yet), x4
Sudden, x4 DI, I won some meaningless 9 player tournament. Got bored
and moved on to Gargoyles with Presence and other life-affirming
sweetness.

Though, I'd actually be more inclined to play more masterkillers than
DIs these days, that is if my decks weren't way too busy using up
master slots to do something ineffectual. Admittedly, I play in a
modest DI meta where the DI deck would have to pull extra weight,
nevermind that it's hard enough for anyone to get ousted without
counterspells flying that it's kind of gratuitous to bog games down
even more.

BTW, the next obvious ban is Anthelios. DI arguably serves some
purpose in the game - enabling players to stop things without having
to find a way to block them*. Anthelios's [interesting] master
filtering value is grossly overshadowed by the recursion engine abuse.

* What happens if you ban DI? Do decks go heavy to extremes of
noninteractivity and superinteractivity, losing the middle ground,
because it becomes sufficiently easy to have sick actions occur that
stopping them requires overloading on intercept or accepting that they
can't be stopped leading to more weenie decks, et al? Would make
bounce more reliable in the post "what do you mean I have to decline
to block to bounce?" world, which may or may not be considered
progress.

Counterspells are just a bad concept both in terms of being antifun
and in terms of enabling a game to get away with other bad concepts.
Once introduced into CCGs, the CCGs build around them - it's not
possible to remove the Suddens/Washes from the world at this point (if
ever). It may not be possible to remove DI. But, then, quite a few
aren't calling for its removal, they are calling for its downgrade.
Very, very hard to see what happens with errata to such a popular
card. As suggested, the cure may be worse than the disease.

Master cards are generally much fewer in a deck, and as a result players
tend to pick the more obviously powerful ones.

There are, of course, exceptions, but IME most plays of master cards are
further towards the "very good" end of the spectrum. Individual minion
card plays may or may not be good at a given moment, but many of the
master cards that are played give the potential for long term gains -
continuous pool gain, continuous defence. Pentex Subversion - already
mentioned - is another very strong card. With only 10-20 master cards
in a deck, each of them may contain significant power. Against good
players, your cancellations will almost always hit good master cards
because they're not playing master cards that aren't very strong - there
are so many strong master cards competing for space.

They may not be so obviously good right at the time - hey look, I play
Govern and get 3 pool, vs I play Blood Doll and get 1 pool. But that
Blood Doll may have a much larger swing over the course of the game.
Add the fact that you can cancel them with an OOT:Trifle (which has
downsides, but is hardly unplayable) and you can interfere quite
significantly.

> Just to fall back to my initial point, why is it that Direct

> (OOT Master, 1 pool), which has a very similar effect, is incredibly

Vox Domini always does what you wanted. They called the political action,
they tapped, we're now voting, boom! If there was a cost to playing the
vote (e.g. Reckless Agitation), it is not recovered. They might have spent
action modifiers getting votes or other advantages like bribes to pass the
referendum. (If they spent a huge amount on an Awe, it's fantastic!)
It fails and their minion stays tapped. It's Delaying Tactics without
it's achilles heal: the recovery of the political action card.

Direct Intervention allows an acting minion to stay untapped. It allows
replay of most minion cards, aside from action modifiers and reactions.
(Most common usage of action modifiers is stealth and reactions either
wake or intercept. Often you can substitute another stealth or intercept
and get the same effect; wake far less so but it's still possible.) It's
more flexible but does decidely less against political actions than VD.

Admittedly, I had a phase where I used Vox Domini in various decks as a
prayer card defense against political actions (especially seat switchers,
still legal at the time). Then I decided to swap them out for DIs for
exactly this reason - flexibility. None the less, I still don't agree
that DI is overpowered.

> One could argue "Cause Vox Domini sucks".

I don't say Vox Domini sucks exactly. It's actually quite a powerful
card when it's playable. It just doesn't make my decks because it's
a defense against something (political actions) which doesn't come up
enough in the game. You can translate that into "Vox Domini sucks"
for these purposes, I guess.

> Or one could look at Vox
> Domini (designed long after Direct Intervention, but a sane design team)
> and say "Huh. DI should probably work like Vox Domini, as that is
> clearly what the current design team thinks is reasonable for a 1 pool
> OOT Master that cancels something..."

I hope not - or 1 pool OOT masters are not likely to get much use
on the whole. But the game has lots of cards in which just weren't given
enough upside in view of their downsides. Even after the design team got
replaced with sane people.

Fred

Lacking the energy to look at all tournaments of 20+ participants in
the last two years, I decided to just look at 50+. In the two 100+,
both from 2007, there are three copies of DI each, both Imbued decks.
In the thirteen 50+ decks, eight of them have zero copies of DI.

the world, there doesn't seem to be a lot to be concerned about.

difficulty getting the cards they cared about.

> decks to tournaments, they are generally just the decks I do well with
> in casual play, and I don't then add DI to them just for competition.
> Maybe if I did, I'd win more :-)

Some of the biases I see in the TWDA that affect trying to analyze it:
a. There are only limited results to where certain groups of players
have an unusually high amount of influence.
b. Within those groups, there tends to be players who win a
disproportionate percentage of the groups' tournaments to where a
small number of individuals around the world have an unusually high
amount of influence.
c. As a believer that decks don't win tournaments, players do, the
TWDA doesn't reflect deck optimization but what a small number of
players in the world have the most success with.

So, I can see this as a possibility. Yet, if the only data we have on
the game doesn't reflect the power of something, especially given that
it's hardly surprising what cards do see the most play in the TWDA
helping to justify that there is something valid in the statistics,
it's hard to come up with any sort of statistical basis for
criticizing a card on a power level.

I think it's justifiable to kill cards based on how obnoxious they are
rather than just purely in terms of how powerful they are, and I can
see where DI would annoy people. But, I don't know how anyone is
justifying an excessive power level for the card. Why not restrict
Conditioning to once per game?

Sure. You're missing the point, however. The effect you describe
may in fact occur and you claim you engage in it and I believe you.
Other motivations may indeed affect peoples' choices for cards in their
tournament decks but how would you ever prove Direct Intervention is
more prone to people irrationally hesitating to use it more than any
other card? Who knows? Who could possibly know?

Since there's no way to gauge hidden motivations as factors when people
_aren't_ using a given card when they have the best incentive to use
that card, they have to be ignored along with all the other freakish
possibilities.

Occam's Razor states that one should assume the simplest possible
explanation for a given observation, in this case that the reason
DI isn't used in higher numbers is generally because it's utility
doesn't merit more usage. Occam's Razor is not a logical proof of
anything as much as a simple discipline of thought; failing such a
discipline, the number of possible theories for Direct Intervention
non-usage are boundless ("secret agents of the Korvian Empire are
placing transmitters in the heads of the best VtES players"). In order
to learn something useful, you have to accept the simplest explanation -
that the tendency to refuse to use a card for some irrational subjective
reason of some sort is pretty much proportional to its popularity as a
strong card. And it all cancels out.

Might not be right. But what's the point in engaging in speculation?
I mean, besides just a general desire to cast doubt on what little
evidence we have about how strong Direct Intervention is - or is not.

> It has nothing to do with embarrassment.

...

> can't possibly be alone in something like this. I'm not saying this has
> any impact at all on whether or not DI is overpowered. Just that it
> might affect how many show up in TWDs, among any number of other reasons.

Embarrassment, irrationality, tendency towards bad hair days. It doesn't
matter what the effect is. If you can't measure it, it's all speculation.
We use the TWDA because we assume people _want_ to win tournaments and
this motivation is ultimately the strongest, averaged over the entire
population. It's understood that such an assumption could be fraught with
hidden anomalies and you have to take it for what it's worth. It just
seems lame to start talking about them only when you're uncomfortable with
what the TWDA actually shows.

Fred

>canceling a minion card, on the other hand, are not as bunched up in
>the middle. Therefore I argue that there are more chances for DI to
>have a game winning effect than for Sudden Reversal.

The DI may look more obviously like a game-winning effect - Yay! I
stopped the bleed for 3! or Yay! I stopped it being bounced to me! -
but stopping the master tech can be just as game winning.

- You don't have that 5 pool from a blood gain master (Doll or Vessel
over several turns, Tap or Tribute right now etc.) so I don't have to
deal with the Assault Rifle you choose not to bring out now.

- Over several turns, I call two Con Boons and gain 8 pool, which would
have been stopped by your KRCG (or the intercept location of your
choice).

- Taking out the Fame or Tension can save me a hunk of pool.

- Taking out an early Power Structure can really slow down a Lasombra
breed-boon deck.

- Taking out a Parthenon may well cause jam issues for a master heavy
deck, until it can draw another.

All of those can radically alter the course of a game, and cause huge
problems for a deck. None of the cards just mentioned is unlikely,
unusual or rarely seen, and there are a variety of similarly strong
cards that other decks will use.

The point is, taking out master cards can be just as game-winning as
taking out minion cards. However, you have to look at long-term gains
as well as short-term gains. Taking out useful master tech can mean
that you don't need the short-term gain later, because the deck isn't in
a position to do what it would have.

What I don't get is why you guys are in such agreement on Vox Domini.
I include it all the time in decks that have an answer to bleed but no
answer for votes. Frex, a Settite "wall" deck with Shemti and
Crocodile Temple and Ecstasy and lot of Temptations - a vote deck
behind me and my whole strategy crumbles. I've waffled back and forth
between Delaying Tactics, Poison Pill, and Touch of Pain for vote
defense (actually considered Dread Gaze for a minute), but I always
keep a Vox Domini in, and it's useful a lot of the time - more useful
than any of the minion cards for stopping votes. It does have a much
higher opportunity cost than DI, but it also fails the vote, leaving
the vampire tapped, instead of just making them play a second copy of
it - and for the few votes with a cost, even better... not to mention
if they've played an Awe for 12 votes too, planning to Voter Cap. If
you're worried about a vote predator, Vox Domini (I can't bring myself
to abbreviate it as VD... that's reserved for Vampiric Disease =))
could be a lot worse. It's not a 1 in every deck card, like DI could
be, but it's not terrible.

As far as DI - yeah, it's a dramatic play a lot of the time, and it
sucks when your lynch-pin card gets cancelled, but whatever. If you
don't have another playable substitute for the card that was
cancelled, you live with it. More than a 3 pool swing is highly
unlikely. I don't see how you can even compare it to PTO cancelling
an entire vampire. In my mind, it's just a substitute for meta-
gaming... not sure what you're going to see, well, a DI can at least
deal with *one* card, even if a cost of 1 pool and a MooT is kind of
high. The only deck I regularly play with DI is No Secrets From
Casewayo, because he simply has no answer for Call of the Hungry Dead
and Elder Intervention. There are some other decks like that too, but
I see DI more often cancelling bounce (was not quite as strong until
it was ruled that you can't bounce until after you decline to block)
or like a Foreshadowing Destruction... strong, but so often you just
have to wait with it in your hand until you see that moment where it
will be very useful. You can say that it's "always" playable, but
when you use it to cancel a maneuver and the guy just plays another,
or some garbage like that, it's simply not worth the cost.

Neither of these were obsolesced by PTO, in the way you're claiming for
Vox Domini and Direct Intervention.

ECU and AdF belong in radically different decks to PTO - different
sects, titles etc. They could be icing on the cake for such a deck, if
you've already made the necessary choices to play a deck where they
could be used. This is unlike VD and DI, where if a deck is capable of
playing one, it's capable of playing the other - at which point, you
decide which one's best.

mono-ECU deck would suck compared to the mono-PTO deck. But you didn't
have to make whole decks based around PTO - 2 or 3 were plenty to cause
issues, even if you could make a playable deck with 8 - and you didn't
have to make a deck solely devoted to ECU.

Fair enough. This is clearly a reasonable way to better understand
both positions.

1) Power curve. My casual decks don't employ tournament mechanics to
attempts to win (e.g. weenie pre/dom bleed, dem/obf bleed). Casual
decks are just that - intended to be competitive, but quirky and quite
frankly, more fun/interesting to play.

Likewise, when others are playing similar decks, me playing (what I
continue to believe is) an "I trump you, you fail" card burdens my
conscience.

Clearly, we disagree on the relative power of DI. My gut tells me two
things.

- You value MPAs far more than I do. I know I run fewer Masters as a
baseline than most people - if I'm at 18, I feel bloated. Therefore,
DI becomes relatively less cumbersome to me.

- From playing with you, my impression is that your decks tend to be
highly repetitive and therefore less subject to incurring penalty from
DI than decks I often build (especially in casual settings). Both
deck styles have merit. The repetitive style is easier to drive - but
gets screwed more often by table seating. No longer being able to
control that aspect of the game, I have found it advantageous to
diversify a bit - and DI definately impacts that part of more toolboxy
construction.

2) Basic game (thematic) design. Masters represent direct influence
from a methesulah. Other master cards should be what cancels those
functions (unless a card is "put in play" as a result, then a minion
action on that card makes sense because is it some type of lingering
manifestation).

Minions exist to act, and to stop other minions from acting.
Methesulahs' direct influence in this game mechanic should be limited,
otherwise why not simply do away with the need for minions and
influence and just act directly? Print a master card that says "burn
10 pool to burn 10 of your prey's pool" and be done with it (yes, I
know, that's way over the top, but it conveys the sentiment).

3) Seeing cool things. I like to see my decks work, and other
peoples' decks work. Blocks are one thing, but when I can just STOP a
linchpin function so easily (and yes, I maintain that an experienced
user of DI does this better than the average player) - then I don't
get to see the other fella's deck do what he spent hours designing.
Certainly, this makes DI good for competitive play - and I remain
competitive even in casual games - but not as much FUN.

Those are the reasons I don't play DI in my 30-some (or more???)
casual decks.

Truth-by-blatant-assertion. You _say_ "the outcome will most likely
become a disaster...(yadda, yadda)" but you don't give any real
evidence that getting DIed is any worse than getting SRed. Sure,
the minion phase has more things in it, so what? That can also mean
you have time to set up your key play to make it difficult to DI to
any meaningful result or that you have time to recover from it,
thus mitigating rather than aggravating the result.

Even assuming it tends to aggravate rather than mitigate (perhaps
because the person playing the DI can do so at a time of his own
choosing), here's a counterargument why getting my key master SRed
is worse: masters, by necessity, need to be played in far fewer
numbers than minion cards. You can usually afford to have a lot of
copies of a key minion card because most of them will be played over
and over. How many Palla Grandes should be placed in an anti-Toreador
bleed deck though? It may be quite a few turns before I draw another
one.

We can argue this way until we're blue in the face. If DI is so over-
powered, build the DI super-deck and win too many tournaments with it
and show us.

> keep a Vox Domini in, and it's useful a lot of the time - more useful
> than any of the minion cards for stopping votes.

Well, there's the short answer - and I did say it earlier, perhaps
you missed it. The way metagames in my area have gone, I just
abandoned the notion of needing vote defense entirely. It's just not
important enough. I do occasionally lose a game on that basis (or if
I don't, I live off someone esle's vote defense) but often enough
whatever my deck _does_ do is often part of the answer anyway. Bleed
it out, attack it, intercept it, or whatever.

If you believe you specifically need vote defense, then sure. Vox
Domini may very well be a worthwhile card.

> As far as DI - yeah, it's a dramatic play a lot of the time, and it
> sucks when your lynch-pin card gets cancelled, but whatever. If you
> don't have another playable substitute for the card that was
> cancelled, you live with it. More than a 3 pool swing is highly
> unlikely. I don't see how you can even compare it to PTO cancelling
> an entire vampire. In my mind, it's just a substitute for meta-
> gaming... not sure what you're going to see, well, a DI can at least
> deal with *one* card, even if a cost of 1 pool and a MooT is kind of
> high. The only deck I regularly play with DI is No Secrets From
> Casewayo, because he simply has no answer for Call of the Hungry Dead
> and Elder Intervention. There are some other decks like that too, but
> I see DI more often cancelling bounce (was not quite as strong until
> it was ruled that you can't bounce until after you decline to block)
> or like a Foreshadowing Destruction... strong, but so often you just
> have to wait with it in your hand until you see that moment where it
> will be very useful. You can say that it's "always" playable, but
> when you use it to cancel a maneuver and the guy just plays another,
> or some garbage like that, it's simply not worth the cost.

Yep.

Fred

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:

> We can argue this way until we're blue in the face.  If DI is so over-
> powered, build the DI super-deck and win too many tournaments with it
> and show us.

Much like we have previously established that the TWDA is not a
completely valid source of data, I think we have previously
established that a card can be broken/overpowered/whatever and not
cause a lot of tournaments to be won with them. For example:

-Anarch Revolt: Its problem was that it was too good at making *other*
people win other than the person playing the Anarch Revolt.

-Succubus Club: Much like Anarch Revolt, it is broken in that it was
really good at making *other* people win (spite "I'm about to get
ousted. I'll give someone across the table all my stuff 'cause I'm at
1 pool and dying anyway...").

Granted, DI is *far* more likely to make you win than either of the
above highly problematic cards, but still, "winning a lot of
tournaments" with something isn't likely to help the argument a lot of
the time.

-Peter

> 1) Power curve. My casual decks don't employ tournament mechanics to

> decks are just that - intended to be competitive, but quirky and quite
> frankly, more fun/interesting to play.

I have something like the same concept - decks I will play in casual
play but wouldn't trust in a tournament. I don't avoid using particular
cards or tactics as being too powerful for casual play because I don't
think playing at lower power level is the point. At least not for me.
For me, the main difference is that a quirky deck is likely to have larger
holes in terms of what its vulnerable to in the metagame or else I'm just
experimenting with something or both. I don't want to get stuck with
such a deck for multiple rounds in a tournament. Since I don't want to
play them in tournaments, casual play is the only other outlet.

> Likewise, when others are playing similar decks, me playing (what I
> continue to believe is) an "I trump you, you fail" card burdens my
> conscience.

I'm not sure why. It sounds to me like you're dancing to ghost music,
trying to guess what's impolite to play in casual company.

I have an anecdote about what I mean. The one time I can ever remember
someone reacting with annoyance to one of my decks in casual play, it
actually turned out to be what I'd consider a quirky casual-play-only
deck I'd never take into tournament. It's a deck that Mind Rapes minions
and puts out Temptations and uses Heidelburg Castle to steal their
resources and hence control opposing players. I played it in a casual
game after a Continental Qualifier a couple years ago and it worked
unusually well against the girlfriend of one of the princes. She was
a pretty good player but apparently got frustrated with a "clamp-down"
tactic and didn't really want to see how vulnerable my deck was to a
million other things that weren't helping her at that moment. (I'd
never play that deck in a tournament. It's actually quite bad.) I'm not
sure what you can do. Maybe I should have saved the deck for players
I know better but in Phoenix, there isn't too much opportunity for that.

The point is, I would never refrain from playing a deck in casual play
out of a fear that it was too good in some way. The above ancedote shows
that you have no idea what's going to bother someone so why try censoring
yourself? This game is supposed to be balanced and I feel it's up to my
opponents to make sure they have a chance in a game, not me. Besides, if
you refuse to play at the highest level, how is someone _else_ going to
gather useful information when they're experimenting? It's like you're
depriving your opponents of knowing if their decks will work in tournaments
where they _will_ run into DIs.

> Clearly, we disagree on the relative power of DI. My gut tells me two
> things.
>
> - You value MPAs far more than I do. I know I run fewer Masters as a
> baseline than most people - if I'm at 18, I feel bloated. Therefore,
> DI becomes relatively less cumbersome to me.

I agree.

> - From playing with you, my impression is that your decks tend to be
> highly repetitive and therefore less subject to incurring penalty from
> DI than decks I often build (especially in casual settings). Both
> deck styles have merit. The repetitive style is easier to drive - but
> gets screwed more often by table seating. No longer being able to
> control that aspect of the game, I have found it advantageous to
> diversify a bit - and DI definately impacts that part of more toolboxy
> construction.

I agree with that, too. Also, I have trouble thinking on my feet a
lot - that is, seeing an unusual play or an unusual opportunity or
the flip side, an unusual danger. This point tends to get aggravated
by the fact that I can't bring myself to play the same deck very often.
(I get bored with the same deck over an over.) I compensate for that
somewhat by using decks with strong, repetitive tactics where I don't
have to think through new situations as much.

> 2) Basic game (thematic) design. Masters represent direct influence
> from a methesulah. Other master cards should be what cancels those
> functions (unless a card is "put in play" as a result, then a minion
> action on that card makes sense because is it some type of lingering
> manifestation).

OK. Not much to say about aethestics. You like what you like.

> 3) Seeing cool things. I like to see my decks work, and other
> peoples' decks work. Blocks are one thing, but when I can just STOP a
> linchpin function so easily (and yes, I maintain that an experienced
> user of DI does this better than the average player) - then I don't
> get to see the other fella's deck do what he spent hours designing.

That's a fair enough reaction. I feel the same way about intercept
decks - the type where someone just sits there and builds up and refuses
to let you do anything unless you can trump his combat (and he has a lot
of combat). I just don't think of it as something where I can go to the
newsgroup and ask to change the game. I mean it is what it is.

I suppose DI is different in that you probably see it as the one card
that, if it were banned, you wouldn't have to worry about the effect any
more. And making the plea on that basis doesn't bother me as long as
it isn't represented as "this-card-is-too-powerful". It isn't. The card
is balanced given its true costs (opportunity and the reactive nature of
the card which may or may not contribute to your position in any particular
game), it's just that it's a defense that can be used in so many different
ways that its use against the most convenient weak spot of a carefully
planned deck offends you.

> Certainly, this makes DI good for competitive play - and I remain
> competitive even in casual games - but not as much FUN.

I actually see it as a fun. It doesn't offend me to see something
terribly clever DIed because I figured that, however clever the original
play was, I also find it clever that a person arranged to be holding a
DI at that particular moment. I enjoy such turns.

Fred

Direct Intervention in casual play is more or less impolite.

> But then if I started doing that, I

> point I have helped create an environment where everyone is playing 3x
> DIs in every deck.

To reiterate something I said to Darby, you don't really know what would
happen if you started playing 3 DIs in every deck. Could be that the
biggest thing that would happen is that your opponents would learn something
they needed to know to play tournaments well. You might also discover that
they have a much more imaginative response to it than you're assuming they'll
have and, just maybe, that Direct Intervention isn't as powerful as you
feared.

Or maybe you're right. I honestly can't say.

Of course, if you're right, then you're also depriving the game of something
"it" needs to know (conceptualizing the massed community of VtES players as
an entity) - that the complaint about DI is totally valid and that, once
established in a place, DI will take over like a weed. Maybe the only reason
places like Los Angeles exist is that too many players are trying to be "nice"
and not play it except a little in tournament play. Who knows? If you try to
deprive others of information by not playing your best game, it could happen.

Competition makes people better - one way or another.

Fred

He's not making excuses. He's pointing out that the TWDA is flawed, and
if you were looking at an objective source of the most powerful decks
EVER, things might be different. The TWDA is not such a source (which
is mostly impossible to get hold of).

Those aren't excuses. They're explanations of the limits of the TWDA.

I'm not sure which part of this you can't get.

TWDA not perfect. Peter: He say TWDA not perfect. Peter: He think:
"What might happen if Ceiling Cat make perfect world?" Peter: He might
be wrong because he is thinking not just looking, but he not making
excuse.

A variety of people clearly don't play DI for a variety of reasons:

- it hasn't been reprinted recently (so it's harder for newbies to have)
- it isn't a card some people like at all because they really feel ick
about playing it (so they don't put it in their decks)
- it's often not used in casual play by some of those players (which can
have knock-on effects to deck-building for competitive play)
- some players make a strategic decision against it (e.g. they'd rather
have a Temptation of Greater Power and a Minion Tap, not 2 DI).

On top of that, you'll have people who are playing DI regularly in
playgroups and who don't see it as a problem.

This is *EXACTLY* like pretty much every other significant card in V:TES
ever. Tomb of Rameses III, Return to Innocence, Thoughts Betrayed...
all of these had some people choosing to play them, and some people
choosing not to play them because they just thought they were wildly
inappropriate, and some people playing them and not seeing any problem
at all. Monocle of Clarity was used in plenty of places without people
trying to enforce a circular question about a question. During every
PTO discussion ever, there were howls of people saying you shouldn't
change it, and other people just choosing not to play it because they
don't like it.

These cards wouldn't, therefore, necessarily turn up in Tournament
Winning Decks in line strictly with their power/utility/cost ratio,
because some players intentionally don't use them - sometimes *because*
they think they're wildly inappropriately broken, and they think using
them in a deck would make them an overly competitive dick when they want
everyone in a playgroup or tournament to have fun. This might happen
especially if the tournament isn't anything too important (like a big
qualifier) - perhaps just the bimonthly meet at a local store with a
dozen people.

One of the situations that occurs reasonably often is a card (or a small
combination of cards) is decried as too powerful. It's usually pointed
out that a seriously useful way to demonstrate this is to take it to a
reasonably sized tournament and do significant damage with it -
repeatedly if possible. Now, clearly, sometimes people won't be able to
do this because the card or combo they're decrying isn't wildly
powerful, inappropriate, or table destroying. But sometimes they don't
want to do it because it involves them trying to cause significant shit
for people at a tournament, and they don't really want to ruin it for
everyone else. So they don't play it. So there's no chance of them
winning with it. So it doesn't turn up in the TWDA. So the TWDA isn't
perfect. So if they'd chosen to play the deck they thought was outright
strongest for them, it might well have been that deck. So the TWDA
might then get a copy of it.

Hence, the TWDA is not a perfect data source for this kind of
discussion. Peter is *not making excuses*. You're imagining that, for
no obvious reason. He is *speculating* about whether DI could or could
not turn up in the TWDA even more often, and whether people might not be
playing it for some reason or other.

Because it's wrong to assume the target has some immediate replacement
for whatever it is you just nuked. That guy getting his Garous
fizzled lost *time*, not pool, not some special prayer resource in his
deck. It just took him a little while longer to get to the next
Garous and by then more defenses were in place than otherwise would
be. Nuking the Bonding (and, no, it is wrong outside of anything but
an idealized thought experiment to just blithely assume they'll have
something as good to play in its place) costs you an *oust*. How many
times have you gone for it, gotten the six pool, and that is the only
way you survived your predator, and often went on to take the table
based on that momentum? It happens. All. The. Time. Frankly I'm
amazed that anybody who's actually seen the card in play at
tournaments disputes this. I'm not jumping on you, but on DI-deniers
generally.

First, as far as I can tell, it took 2 DI's to make him lose a "turn",
which is actually not even true if he had anything else to do... like
a cheap bleed if you're so sure that he couldn't possibly have been
blocked without a DI. If a single DI makes you lose an entire *turn*,
then you must want to ban Legwork too because that 2 cap with no
animalism or auspex that you were sure couldn't get any intercept can
pay just 1 blood to make you lose your entire turn! Oh, and I bet you
really, really hate Special Report. DI makes you lose a card. That
swing could be a few pool this way or that, or an action that you
didn't think would be blocked otherwise. But it doesn't make you lose
a turn except in exceedingly rare and contrived situations.

> Nuking the Bonding (and, no, it is wrong outside of anything but
> an idealized thought experiment to just blithely assume they'll have
> something as good to play in its place) costs you an *oust*.

And it's wrong to assume that they *won't* have anything good to play
instead. You remember and get pissed off when you don't have a backup
plan, but for every time you get DI'd and don't have another +bleed in
hand, there's another time when your Bonding doesn't get DI'd even
though you have a Threats to back it up with.

If DI'ing a Bonding costs an oust in a particular situation, then so
too would a Telepathic Counter, a Wake and some intercept, a bounce, a
cross-table Folderol or the chimerstry card (Ignis Fatuus? I
forget...) that reduces a bleed against any methuselah by 1. So would
a Life Boon, a Major Boon, an Eagle's Sight.... etc... These cards
all have considerably lower costs than a DI and in most cases would
have been *better* as they negate the possibility of just playing
another card for +bleed. I won't even mention the minion cards that
cancel card plays.

> How many
> times have you gone for it, gotten the six pool, and that is the only
> way you survived your predator, and often went on to take the table
> based on that momentum?  It happens.  All.  The.  Time.  Frankly I'm
> amazed that anybody who's actually seen the card in play at
> tournaments disputes this.   I'm not jumping on you, but on DI-deniers
> generally.
>

And how many times have I gone for it, got blocked or bounced when I
thought he was out of wakes, or a Telepathic Counter just barely saves
him, or a cross-table Boon or Eagle's Sight, etc., etc., etc... When
you lunge, you risk the possibility that you might not make it. If
you don't oust your prey on a lunge, you pretty much lose. This has
nothing to do with DI. It happens. All. The. Time. With DI or
without it.

The only differences between DI and the other means of countering what
you're trying to do are a) the cost - DI costs way more than pretty
much any other means of defense, a pool is one thing, but playing a
MooT is a pretty high cost on its own; and b) the versatility. I
admit it's a lot easier to cancel a bleed card, some stealth, a block-
fails, a voter cap, an action occasionally... with one card than to
try and include the counters for each one separately. But that's why
you have to pay more for it.

Personally, considering the strength of master cards compared to
minion cards and the fact that I only get 1 MPA by default, I'm way
more upset when I get Sudden Reversaled than when I get a card DI'd.
And SR doesn't even cost a pool.

How do you know that? Have you done a quantified study? Or is it just
that you particularly remember the incidents where it plays out that way?
Would you even know how long people wait with the card in hand to make a
play like this? Would you notice when players discard DIs because they
drew multiples or they just don't want the card in hand at that moment for
whatever reason? (These last two sentences highlight why the cost of
playing a DI may well justify even the sensationally good results, when
they're obtained.) This is the trouble I have with anecdotal arguments like
this. Especially when I don't personally experience the same thing. (Or
even if I had, that would still prove nothing because many others may not
have.)

> I guess you've heard all this before and weren't persuaded.

True, but beside the point. Where you quoted me above, I wasn't talking
about disagreeing with the original premise as much as how the original
premise might be proved or disproved. People will tend to be persuaded
about whatever they've experienced but, also for some people, what they
want to believe about the card. Some people, I believe, are more annoyed
by how the card works than whether it's balanced or not. I can't prove
that, either, but the point is that there needs to be some form of
objective observations about the card's popularity and strength of its
benefits or else you're down to fun-ness argument.

Make no mistake, a fun-ness argument might be sufficient if it bothers
enough people to outweigh the value of having it in the game and the PITA
caused by removing it from the game. But if that's the argument, then
call it a fun-ness argument and let's go from there. I'm sick and tired
of people just blatantly asserting that it's overpowered without offering
any kind of objective proof.

Semantic gymnastics would suggest I'm playing with word definitions to
avoid the truth. You're certainly welcome to clear up whatever semantic
issues you have in order to reduce our issues to well-understood ones. But

Well, no offense Fred, since I pretty much agree with you (though I
wouldn't care much if DI were made 1 per game per methuselah - I just
don't think it's ban material, nor is it likely to go 1 per game
either, IMHO), but proof isn't really possible. Aside from something
like the canonical broken master card "oust your prey", it's not
really possible to prove anything is broken a priori. Even something
like "10 pool - Your prey loses 10 pool", though we could agree that
it would be broken, couldn't really be proven as broken, outside of
anecdotal evidence in play if it were ever printed.

You can't even really argue a proof based on being better than another
card. Something like a master card that said "Gain 1 pool. You may,
if you wish, choose one of your predator's or prey's vampires to gain
1 blood" would be strictly better than Ascendance, but the added
effect is so unlikely to be useful that there's no way it could be
considered broken.

There's no proof to be had. Direct Intervention *could be* broken and
there wouldn't be concrete proof, because what would you really
consider proof? Showing up in a lot of tournament winning decks? I
can say that DI probably shows up in a lot more tournament decks than
PTO ever did, and probably as many as Return to Innocence (though I'm
not sure any good records were kept of a time when RtI was tournament
legal), but that's not really proof either.

See, that's the point I am trying to make. Your implication seems to
be that if you can't play all seven cards in your hand at will to full
effect, your entire turn is ruined. In certain outlying instances
this is true. In most cases, DI causes a swing not unlike any other
reasonably powerful card. DI can cause a swing of 3 pool and
determine or prevent an oust, well so can Conditioning and
Deflection. DI just costs more. Putting DI in a deck, to me, is like
putting in a card that could be any one of a number of reaction or
prevention cards, but instead of playing with one of those cards, you
go for flexibility at a much increased cost. When I build a deck, DI
only goes in if there is a specific reason I need it (like DI'ing
Elder Intervention in a No Secrets deck, or DI'ing bleed mods or
bounce in a deck that has no real bleed defense and doesn't think that
Archon Investigation is defensive enough) - I would use it for other
things in those decks, the flexibility is nice, but just flexibility
isn't worth it to me without a specific goal. To me, it sounds like
your other group played DI's like crazy not because they made their
decks win, but because they didn't have a firm grasp on what they
wanted to cancel and so just went for the shotgun blast. It may not
be overpowered in that it makes people win all the time, but it does
sound like not a lot of fun. Unfortunately, there are a lot of cards
in the game that won't make you win but will make life hell for your
opponents. They can't all be banned. Granted, I wouldn't be upset
with DI getting a reprint to "once per game per methuselah", but I
doubt it will happen.

> don't think it's ban material, nor is it likely to go 1 per game
> either, IMHO), but proof isn't really possible.

Complete and total proof isn't, no. But I mean, "proof" as in something
other than just, "I think this card is too flexible" or "a bunch of
people I play with pack several of them in every deck". Something that
indicates the card actually _is_ too powerful.

> There's no proof to be had.

Sure there is. The TWDA gives an indication of which cards are effective
by showing which cards tournament winners do and do not use and in what
numbers and possibly reveals patterns about their use. Anecdotal
evidence _might_ reveal something interesting if the anecdotes were
remarkable, especially if taken from remarkable situations like Continental
Championships or as demonstrations of card power in particularly challenging
situations - just that no one has offered anything that is all that remarkable
in this case.

I think proof could be found if DI were as broken as people claim. I
think the problem is that DI just isn't broken. No card in the game is at
that moment. That's why standards of objective evidence appear to be so
high as to look impossible.

Fred

question is whether your personal standards for what consistitutes an
overpowered card are correct or not. There are at least two guys on this

overpowered, yet they play in the same Los Angeles tournaments I in which
I play and I haven't the faintest idea what they're talking about. It
might be that I haven't seen some other element of play in which they

That's because very few of them actually are. In fact, of all the cards
which have been banned over the years or reduced in power by reprinting/
errata, almost all of them have some other type of problem associated with
them besides just power. PTO was definitely a fun-ness problem. Memories
of Mortality and Edge Explosion just encouraged too many defensive Hunter
decks; neither of these cards are actually overpowered in and of themselves
as much as they contributed to a deck archetype which itself isn't exactly
overpowered either but is just too difficult for too many vampire decks to
oust. While I am assured that reprinted Succubus Club was proved over-
powered, I never saw it in action and there was a side problem that it
caused too much discussion during game. Seat switchers interfered with
the predator-prey relationships in the game.

(Not bothering to talk about Madness of the Bard or ante cards...) Of
all of the banned cards, only Return to Innocence really qualifies as a
flat-out, "This card is too good!"

You can add Tomb of Ramses III and Anarch Revolt as cards that were "banned"
by being altered enough to effectively ban their old forms. ToR3 was another
one, like Return to Innocence, that was just flat out too good. Anarch
Revolt is like most of the cards on the banned list; not really overpowered
but just causing a particular fun-ness or other kind of problem.

You're right that I don't think many of these cards can be considered
bannable on pure power arguments. Some of them are definitely suspicious -
more suspicious by a long shot than DI - but none of them struck me as over
the top when they got banned.

Maybe, by way of comparison, if someone could make some argument that DI
creates some sort of other problem besides just pure power then I could
be persuaded. The potential for cross-table use doesn't do it, though.
Lots of cards have pretty potent cross-table effects. The argument that
gets my attention are the gaming groups where its use is so ubitiqous that
people report massive frustration playing games gets my attention. But I
can't get people to talk about or think about why the card is so popular
in those groups vs. other places. Saying everyone in the group is corrupted
by the card's power isn't going to explain it.

Fred

So, how many tournaments did they win? Any majors?

Multiplayer CCGs really aren't suited to people who are into breaking
games - too many results created by things out of their control. So,
I can see them moving on, one wonders why they ever took the game up
in the first place if they were just going to play it like a two-
player CCG, but that's irrelevant. But, if you are really into
breaking a CCG, then it needs to be done on some sort of stage, the
bigger the better. Even someone who dominates local play, I think,
has something to prove on a larger stage to justify either superior
decktech or superior skill or both.

It's suggestive that DI shows up in such a high percentage of TWDs to
where it may approach staple level. But, even if you took it as a
(one-of) staple card, what of the numerous other staples? Why not
call for the weakening of Deflection and Govern, Blood Doll and Minion
Tap, WWEF and On the Qui Vive, Majesty, Freak Drive, KRC, et al? What
about cards like Heart of Nizchetus, a much, much harder card
(therefore, a card better argued as being only limitedly available)
that shows up in an impressive percentage of decks (per extrala's
blog's stats)?

My observation with niche CCGs is that tech doesn't proliferate as
much as it should, that there tend to be many and occasionally strong
regional biases. So, it's not impossible that someone has found break
points in a game that should be obvious to everyone. But, the game's
managers are going to care about what is having a widespread impact on
the interest in the game. Errata and bannings always tick off
somebody and are bad PR, so there has to be enough clear gain to cause
someone to take action. My suggestion to anyone who wants to get DI
messed with is to play, or find someone to play, in a lot of
tournaments LSJ is at with decks full of DIs and see if they can
either win disproportionately or screw games up disproportionately.

> tournament WoW:CCG. Their idea of fun was "let's break this puppy."

> knife to a gun fight.

So that gives me the picture of players who were very talented in many
ways - more so than just, "Let's use DI." Is it possible that DI was
just part of the picture? Did you suddenly start winning your share
when you started packing 3+ DIs per deck?

I'm always hard pressed to explain just what it is about the guys in LA
that make them better players. All the intercept annoyed the hell out
of me and it's taken me a long time to start getting my mind around what
it actually meant and how to counter it. (It hasn't helped that they
get a lot of play time with other great players - each other - while I
go home and get relatively little time with less talented and particularly
less experienced players between the various tournament weekends.) Over
the years I've often believed this game is too much intercept in part
because of my experiences there. But there's a bunch of balance points
that it's taken me a lot of time to discover existed, let alone how to
choose a good balance.

> Not sure what else you want to talk about regarding this, but maybe if
> you asked a more specific question I could answer it.

Well, I guess it just gets back to what it is you found frustrating
about playing against DIs. Some of the points Chris Berger is touching
on are kind of my bone of contention as well. Your idea (and Darby's and
certainly other people) that VtES comes down to certain key plays that make
or break a game or at least generate huge swings in power is probably not
unreasonable. It can be an opponent getting a problematic permanent on
the board (e.g. No Secrets or Aranthebes), rushing someone, or a big bleed,
or the stealth/intercept contests over these, or the bouncing of the bleed
or a lot of things. The issue, interpreted in my own words, is the
flexibility of DI which makes it that one extra relevant card in the
contest which can thereby decide the matter. In the matter of the Garou
permanents which started this thread, a player was apparently holding
two Garou near the beginning of the game before an opponent could set up
his problematic Prince/intercept defense, yet two early DIs canceled them
both and thus proved decisive in the game. That a master can be flexible
enough to counter any single minion in the game (as long as it isn't the
player's turn and as long as the player hasn't already played an OOT since
his last turn) seems to be the complaint.

(Some people also complain about the availability for cross-table
involvement allowed by the card but I believe this is much easier
to dismiss given how many cards have an element of that.)

I think that different people are estimating the contribution of the
DI card differently. It depends on whether you focus on the fact
that DI changed the result - when it changes the result - or the fact
that it's often just one of many factors, all equally involved in
changing the result. Had that guy opened the game with _three_ Garou
in hand, it's unlikely we would be having this debate. More likely,
had one of his two opponent _not_ been holding a DI card at the time,
the Garou player would have gotten his first one out and things would
have been much different. So it's not just DIs, it's the Garou cards that
mattered. In other examples, an extra stealth or intercept (admittedly
having to be a different card than the DIed card) or a different kind
of bounce in hand will change a result. DIs allow results to get
changed but only under specific circumstances. Yet their costs (like
blood spend for a stealth card) always apply whether they change a
result or not.

So if I've analyzed this right, the question boils down to which
is more important, the flexibility of DI or the cost? And how often
DI actually makes a difference bears heavily on the perception as
well. I think this is where people vary greatly in their perception
of the card.

As to why it's so frustrating in some environments, I can't say
since I haven't had the experience. My speculation is that people
remember better what they get frustrated from trying and failing
than what they stop others from doing. Or it might be the same
frustration I feel trying to play draft tournaments where making
plays that advance the game along is much more difficult than in
constructed play. Or both. Or something else. I don't know.

Fred
