Sure. Any intercept card. It doesn't do exactly that particular set
of things but it can make any action in the game fail.

Of course, it's only potentially one card in a card war with the
stealth or other things the actor could play to rescue the situation
but so is Direct Intervention: actions and combat cards can be replayed,
action modifiers and reactions that got canceled are harder but can
be substituted for in many situations, and the situation can likewise
be saved against a DI. Are they exactly equal? No - nor should they
be given DI's unique cost and the limitation inherent in an OOT master.
For that reason, your stab at showing that DI possesses some over the
top benefit is not proved.

Just to be clear, _any_ reactive-type effect in a CCG has to be more
flexible than the proactive effect(s) against which it's used and/or
it has to provide some unusual or extreme benefit or it wouldn't - on
balance - be worth using. Just how flexible or beneficial that should
be exactly isn't clear and is debatable and this certainly leaves room
for the opinion that DI is over the top anyway. But some people aren't
always clear on that point, so I like to mention it from time to time.

Fred

Direct Intervention does several things that are bad for the game:

1) It gives Methuselahs a chance to totally wreck the predator/prey
relationship at almost any given moment. Sudden Reversal is less
problematic because it's actually Methuselahs dueling over resources
at that point. Plus Master cards are much less frequently played than
minion cards.

2) It gives Methuselahs a power equivalent to the best defense of any
minion card. Need to stop that stealth or intercept? Done. Need to
stop that political action? Done. Need to stop that once per combat
card? Done. It obviously and by design trumps any minion card, but is
that really necessary?

3) It benefits reactive decks or slow disproportionately because they
naturally use a significant portion cards on opponent's turns.
Intercept is becoming problematic in some circles. Jay Kristoff's
Auspex weenie deck and imitators have had massive success in recent
history.

4) It will cut down on negotiations and time-wasting during a game.
Too often someone is holding a DI (or bluffing) and trying to work
some sort of a deal. Some say jokingly that "the cheating phase never
ends" but we all know that in reality it's "the DI phase that never
ends."

I think those reasons are sufficient to ban the card. We got rid of
seat changing votes due to #1 and DI clearly violates predator/prey.

Now, the more interesting thing in my mind is what happens *after* DI
is banned. We will actually truly and finally determine what cards are
the most detrimental for VTES's long-tem health. Una Freak Drive decks
may become rampant because DI is one of the few trumps to that deck.
Stealth bleed could become more powerful because intercept decks can't
stop a key action modifier. Large cap voters could benefit from no
counters to Voter Captivation or once-per-game power political
actions. Immortal Grapple combat would also become stronger. But as
long as Direct Intervention is part of the game, true card strength
evaluation will remain artful guesswork.

Recently we (me, Ira Fay, Chris Shorb, Nat Hammond, and Rob Williams)
banned DI in a small series of online games at JOL. Those games have
become much more interesting with that single card banned. In almost
all respects, the tables have collapsed just as they should. Once one
player is hurting, they almost inevitably have crumbled because they
didn't have the resources to help themselves. This I think is good for
the game. No miraculous saves from some cross-table "angel" who is
meddling too much in others' affairs.

Now, I do like some of the newer "cancel" cards which have hit the
scene: Approximation of Loyalty, False Resonance, Hide the Mind,
Scalpel Tongue, Tangle Atropos' Hand, etc. These keep in the spirit of
the disciplines and encourage offense and ousting. I wouldn't even
mind if there were more cancel reactions like Power of One. They all
have requirements and keep in the theme of the game. This is a good
road to travel. Hopefully we've walked far enough down this road to
get rid of "the crutch" once and for all.

Jeff

if you can get a unique permanent in play and it doesn't expend itself

very powerful but had limitations on it that kept it from being an over-
powered crutch card with which to win games just by throwing lots of them
in your deck.

switchers did.

> the game and you do not need to pack a shitload of them for that to
> happen.

Yea, but what bugs me about the argument is that there's so many holes
in it. DI helps you win what I've been referring to as a "card war" -
an exchange of one guy trying to do a thing and someone else trying to
stop him doing that thing. Sometimes it might involve a big-bleed vs. an
intercept-and-pummel-in-combat kind of decision point but usually it's
not that dramatic a difference. It's an incredibly flexible card but
it's still only one card in those wars so if you pick the wrong moment
to use it, it doesn't help and the MPA cost is kind of steep for a miss
like that. I guess if you're good enough at picking your moment it
might make an unusual difference but it hasn't been my experience that
people can. I thought seat switchers were _much_ easier to predict
when you could use them to roll up a game. PTO was, too, if you want
to insist that it was overpowered. And both of those cards didn't have
anything like the same cost as DI, whether you're successful or not.

Fred

> I certainly hope we do not re-open a debate that is now moot, but I
> want to note that not everyone agrees with your assertion that PTO was
> merely a fun problem, not a power problem. I'm sure you've heard it
> before, but I think noting that PTO burns a vampire in one card,
> compared to how difficult that is to do in combat, is a good
> argument. In turn, I have heard the counter-arguments about other
> cards that burn vampires. We stand where we stand, but I think PTO
> was also a balance problem.

Sure. I'm not claiming a community consensus on that one. But there are
some distinct parallels here:

1) Long periods of time in which both cards have stayed legal, had their
haters, and inspired long contentious threads despite the fact that no
particular new tech had been created to exploited their power over the
years. (This contrasts with, for instance, Succubus Club.)

2) Lack of evidence that use of the card was becoming more ubiquitous over
time. This is probably easier for a "general" plug-it-in-anywhere card
like DI than a card like PTO which only drops into a specialized deck. You
could point at the popularity of Inner Circle (particularly Arika) decks
to judge it but, unfortunately, there's so many other considerations that
it tends to lead to arguments that go in circles. At least, say, the deck
archetype that used PTO wasn't horribly overrepresented and I don't get the
sense that people have abandoned Inner Circle members because PTO is gone -
for what it's worth.

3) The evidence against PTO seems to totally rely on the same type of
evidence being lodged against DI: simple assertion that it's effect is too
powerful based entirely on discussions of card mechanics. Well, OK, some
people like Peter seem to think the number of them which show up in the
TWDA buttresses their position but I sure don't.

There is one difference, though. I didn't mourn the loss of PTO overmuch.
While not overpowered, having it played on you usually ruined your game and
that's not good thing for the game. More to the point in this discussion,
it didn't strike me as doing anything useful in the game. Inner Circle
members have plenty of other strengths, they didn't need PTO. I agree with
certain other people here who have posted that DI has a few important functions
in terms of being a defense-of-last-resort for certain kinds of decks against
certain types of opposing strategies. I think someone used the term, "evening
out" which is appropriate.

Fred
